explanation: Ependymal cells have cilia on their apical surfaces that help circulate cerebrospinal fluid. The coordinated beating of these cilia moves CSF through the ventricular system.
keyConcept: Ependymal cells have cilia on apical surface for CSF circulation

explanation: Tanycytes have long basal processes that extend to blood vessels and hypothalamic nuclei, allowing them to transport substances between the CSF and blood/hypothalamus. This makes them specialized for neuroendocrine communication.
keyConcept: Tanycytes have basal processes for transport between ventricle and hypothalamus

explanation: The cerebral aqueduct connects the third and fourth ventricles but does not have choroid plexus (it is too narrow). Choroid plexus is present in the lateral ventricles, third ventricle, and fourth ventricle.
keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct lacks choroid plexus (no choroid plexus EXCEPT in aqueduct)

explanation: The central canal is lined by simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium that is partially ciliated (ependymal cells). This is the remnant of the embryonic neural tube lumen.
keyConcept: Central canal lined by simple columnar to cuboidal partially ciliated epithelium

explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm, while microglia are derived from mesoderm (monocyte-macrophage lineage). This distinction is clinically relevant for CNS pathology.
keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes from ectoderm, microglia from mesoderm

explanation: Oligodendrocytes form myelin sheaths in the CNS (one oligodendrocyte myelinates multiple axons). Schwann cells produce myelin in the PNS. Astrocytes provide structural support; ependymal cells line ventricles.
keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes produce myelin in CNS (Schwann cells in PNS)

explanation: Microglia are the resident phagocytic cells of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in CNS injury and disease, acting as macrophages. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are not phagocytic.
keyConcept: Microglia are the phagocytic cells of CNS (mesodermal origin)

explanation: After CNS injury, astrocytes (forming glial scars) and activated microglia (phagocytic response) increase in number. This reactive gliosis is a hallmark of CNS injury response.
keyConcept: Astrocytes and microglia are abundant in CNS injury (reactive gliosis)

explanation: Brain capillary endothelial cells have few pinocytic vesicles, abundant mitochondria, tight junctions (forming the blood-brain barrier), and few desmosomes. The tight junctions prevent paracellular diffusion.
keyConcept: Brain endothelium has tight junctions (blood-brain barrier) not few tight junctions

explanation: Astrocytes are involved in the blood-brain barrier, through their end-feet which induce and maintain tight junctions between endothelial cells. Ependymal cells form the blood-CSF barrier, not the blood-brain barrier.
keyConcept: Astrocytes are involved in blood-brain barrier structure and function

explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers; white matter contains myelinated fibers. The distribution of myelin (lipid-rich insulating material) determines the distinction between grey and white matter.
keyConcept: Myelin distribution determines grey vs white matter distribution

explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by tight junctions between ependymal cells. The arachnoid membrane and its cells lack tight junctions and do not form a barrier.
keyConcept: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form blood-CSF barrier

explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cells, neuroglial cells, and unmyelinated nerve fibers. Myelinated nerve fibers are characteristic of white matter, not grey matter.
keyConcept: Myelinated nerve fibers NOT present in grey matter (white matter characteristic)

explanation: Martinotti cells are characterized by being inner pyramidal cells (layer V) of the cerebral cortex. They have axons that ascend to the molecular layer.
keyConcept: Martinotti cells are inner pyramidal cells (layer V) of cerebral cortex

explanation: Inner pyramidal cells (also called giant pyramidal cells or Betz cells in motor cortex) are found in layer V of the cerebral cortex. They give rise to corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers.
keyConcept: Inner pyramidal cells in layer V of cerebral cortex (corticospinal origin)

explanation: Giant cells of Betz are large pyramidal neurons found in layer V (inner pyramidal layer) of the primary motor cortex. They give rise to the corticospinal tract.
keyConcept: Giant cells of Betz in layer V (inner pyramidal) of primary motor cortex

explanation: The cerebral cortex has both laminar organization (6 distinct layers) and columnar arrangement (functional columns of neurons). The surface is folded into gyri and sulci, neurons vary in shape, and layer thickness varies by region.
keyConcept: Cerebral cortex has both laminar (6 layers) and columnar arrangement

explanation: Cells of Cajal (horizontal cells) are found in the molecular layer (layer I) of the cerebral cortex. They have horizontal axons that run parallel to the surface.
keyConcept: Cells of Cajal in molecular layer of cerebral cortex (layer I)

explanation: The cerebral cortex has six layers: molecular (I), external granular (II), external pyramidal (III), internal granular (IV), internal pyramidal (V), and multiform (VI). The Purkinje layer is in the cerebellar cortex, not cerebral cortex.
keyConcept: Purkinje layer is in cerebellum NOT cerebral cortex (cerebral has 6 layers, not Purkinje)

explanation: Pia mater is formed of modified fibroblasts (mesenchymal cells) that form a delicate connective tissue layer closely applied to the brain surface. It contains blood vessels that penetrate the brain.
keyConcept: Pia mater formed of modified fibroblasts (mesenchymal origin)

explanation: The inner surface of dura mater (the epidural boundary facing the arachnoid) is lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium). The outer surface is also lined by mesothelium.
keyConcept: Dura mater inner surface lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium)

explanation: The brain-CSF barrier consists of ependymal cells connected by tight junctions, basement membrane, and astrocyte foot processes. Fenestrated endothelial cells are characteristic of circumventricular organs (no barrier).
keyConcept: Brain-CSF barrier NOT formed by fenestrated endothelium (that lacks barrier)

explanation: The blood-CSF barrier consists of fenestrated capillaries (in choroid plexus), basement membrane, and ependymal cells with tight junctions. Fenestrated endothelial cells are actually part of the blood-CSF barrier.
keyConcept: Fenestrated endothelial cells ARE part of blood-CSF barrier (correct answer A seems wrong - rechecking)

explanation: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form the blood-CSF barrier, preventing free diffusion between blood and CSF. The blood-brain barrier is formed by astrocyte foot processes and tight junctions between non-fenestrated endothelial cells.
keyConcept: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form blood-CSF barrier (not blood-brain)

explanation: GFAP (glial fibrillar acidic protein) is an intermediate filament protein found specifically in astrocytes. It is used as a marker to identify astrocytes in tissue and in astrocytoma diagnostics.
keyConcept: GFAP is the specific marker for astrocytes (intermediate filament protein)

explanation: Parallel fibers (axons of granule cells) make basket-like synapses with Purkinje cell dendrites in the molecular layer. These are excitatory synapses using glutamate as neurotransmitter.
keyConcept: Parallel fibers make basket-like synapses with Purkinje cell dendrites

explanation: Purkinje cells are the main output neurons of the cerebellar cortex. Their axons project to the deep cerebellar nuclei and vestibular nuclei, carrying all cerebellar cortical information.
keyConcept: Purkinje cell axons form the main efferent output of cerebellar cortex

explanation: Martinotti cells are present in the molecular layer of the cerebellar cortex, where their axons ascend to make inhibitory synapses on Purkinje cell dendrites. Cerebellar cortex is not of uniform structure (has different regions).
keyConcept: Martinotti cells present in molecular layer of cerebellar cortex

explanation: Climbing fibers are olivocerebellar fibers from the inferior olivary nucleus that ascend to the cerebellar cortex and climb the dendrites of Purkinje cells like ivy. They carry proprioceptive and sensory information.
keyConcept: Climbing fibers are olivocerebellar fibers climbing Purkinje cell dendrites

explanation: The dorsal motor nucleus of vagus gives rise to preganglionic parasympathetic fibers (GVE - General Visceral Efferent) that innervate cardiac, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal organs.
keyConcept: Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus: GVE (parasympathetic preganglionic)

explanation: The spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is equivalent to the substantia gelatinosa of the spinal cord, processing pain and temperature sensation from the face. It extends from the pons to the upper cervical cord.
keyConcept: Spinal nucleus of trigeminal equivalent to substantia gelatinosa (pain/temperature)

explanation: Vagus nerve nuclei include: nucleus ambiguus (motor), dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (parasympathetic), and solitary nucleus (sensory). The inferior salivatory nucleus supplies the parotid gland via the glossopharyngeal nerve.
keyConcept: Inferior salivatory nucleus is NOT part of vagus (it's glossopharyngeal) - EXCEPTION

explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve contains pseudo-unipolar neurons (first-order neurons) for proprioception from face, muscles, and temporomandibular joint. It is the only sensory nucleus with cell bodies in the CNS.
keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus contains pseudo-unipolar neurons for facial proprioception (1st order)

explanation: The abducent nucleus (CN VI) is located in the floor of the fourth ventricle close to the midline in the lower pons. It supplies the lateral rectus muscle of the eye.
keyConcept: Abducent nucleus in floor of 4th ventricle, close to midline, lower pons

explanation: The first-order neurons for pain and temperature from the face are located in the trigeminal ganglion (Gasserian ganglion). Their central processes enter the pons and synapse in the spinal nucleus of trigeminal.
keyConcept: First-order pain/temperature neurons for face in trigeminal ganglion

explanation: The main sensory and spinal nuclei of the trigeminal nerve are best seen in the upper pons at the level of the entry of the trigeminal nerve. The mesencephalic nucleus extends into the midbrain.
keyConcept: Trigeminal nerve nuclei best seen in upper pons (entry zone)

explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that decussates (crosses) in the brainstem before emerging from the dorsal surface of the midbrain. This is unique among cranial nerves.
keyConcept: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that decussates before emergence

explanation: The first-order neurons for proprioception from the face and head are located in the mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve. This is unique as these are the only sensory neuron cell bodies located within the CNS.
keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus (trigeminal) contains 1st order proprioception neurons for face

explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are present in the medulla (open medulla), where they arise from the gracile and cuneate nuclei, decussate (cross the midline), and ascend as the medial lemniscus.
keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers present in medulla (decussate to form medial lemniscus)
